content:
In computer security, a Side-channel attack is one that, rather than taking on the system directly, learns about the inside of the system by observing public activities outside of the security boundary, which leak the internal state of the system.

Humans have been using similar techniques to learn about the insides of human systems for a long time.

There are obvious examples, like inferring an interest in bomb-making when a non-farmer buys vast amounts of fertilizer, or that there’s a story when someone responds peculiarly to a particular person’s name or takes up hobbies that don’t match their normal interests, or that someone wearing dark glasses might have a hangover (or, dark circles around their eyes because they’re in the middle of a 20+ kilometer run).

But I think one of the most common, useful, and high-bandwidth side-channel attacks is imitation.

There’s unconscious imitation, aka mirroring, which seems to help people build rapport. And then there’s imitation proper, which has its own Wikipedia page, mostly concerning toddlers.

The cool thing about imitation is that it’s egalitarian. Many businesses and artists try to hide their “trade secrets”. But you can’t hide who you are, and who you are is your most important trade secret.

But apart from secrets in the sense of things people don’t want you to know, there are things that are secret because they can’t be described: tacit knowledge and ways of being.

In an ideal world, we would be able to climb into someone else’s head to understand them, and what they know. By spending a lot of time with someone (or their work), we can just barely start to approach this. But even if you have a mentor who wants to be able to transfer all their knowledge, often imitation is more efficient than trying to “reach the brain through the ears” (to use Adam Mastroianni’s phrase).

In my experience, imitation is one of the fastest ways to learn.

With many skills, it’s possible to copy the sequence of actions, without it ever “clicking”. Imitation copies the attitude, which tends to make everything else fall into place.

Any time you find a person that you would like to be more like, you can just imitate their outward behaviour, and, chances are, if done accurately enough, it will give insight into the state of mind that leads to that style of behaviour. Imitation can include physical behaviour, like how they walk and sit, but also speech patterns, taste in music and films, their daily habits, how they dress, writing style — which may parallel thinking style — and the shape of their life script at a macro scale.

Writers sometimes physically type out passages from their favourite books in order to learn from them, and get into the headspace of the author.

Imitation is so effective that many cultures attempt to ban it in various contexts. Generally, you aren’t allowed to imitate officials, for example. [From my research for an art project, you aren’t allowed to wear a Canadian police cap in Canada unless you’re a police officer, but you can wear the uniforms for other countries’ police; I haven’t tried this and might be incorrect, so this is not legal advice.]. Still, while you might not be able to imitate a king to his face, nobody’s stopping you from doing it in private.

Often, it seems like there’s a forcing function: outfit → posture → mindset → skill. The research mostly failed to replicate, but this idea has been around for a long time. Maybe there's something to it.

There often seem to be bidirectional feedback loops between the mind and the body. But I find it’s generally easier to bootstrap from the physical to the mental, rather than the other way around.

Also: I find it’s easier to go through the whole chain, and try to become the kind of person who is good at the skill, than to try to jump straight to being good at the skill.

You have to be careful, though, because imitating someone tends to copy both their good and bad qualities. You can’t really imitate the skill without imitating them.

“We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be.”
― Kurt Vonnegut, Mother Night
